## Conclusion

Washington's program expanded who is covered much further than who takes leave, and most of that distance sits at the eligibility rule rather than at the moment of claiming. Workers earning under $19 an hour are 20 percent of the state's workers, 10 percent of those with qualifying work history and 8 percent of paid claimants, and the department puts about 80 percent of that shortfall at eligibility [1]. A separate rule decides whether the job is there afterwards, and 15.5 percent of the lowest earnings quintile qualified for it against 70.4 percent of the highest [2][3]. The strongest contrary reading — that the gap measures different needs rather than a barrier — is engaged below: it accounts for much of the eligibility gap and less for what happens at the bottom once leave is taken [2][5].

## Key findings

- Eligibility turns on 820 hours in the qualifying period, the first four of the last five completed quarters; 74 percent of covered workers are estimated to meet it [2][3].
- Insufficient hours was the largest single denial reason in FY2025, appearing in 38 percent of denied applications [1].
- Replacement is most generous at the bottom: 90 percent of a wage at or below half the state average, then 90 percent of that half plus 50 percent of the excess [3].
- Job protection is a separate rule with separate tests, and 53 percent of eligible workers qualified: 15.5 percent of the lowest earnings quintile against 70.4 percent of the highest, and 25 percent in accommodation and food services against over 76 percent in utilities [2].
- Self-employed workers are covered only if they elect in for three years and pay the whole employee premium; about 10,300 had by mid-2025 [1][3].

## The strongest counterargument

The strongest case that access did expand, and that the gap measures something other than a barrier, is that low-wage jobs carry shorter tenure, fewer hours and more part-year work, so fewer of those workers reach a qualifying event while eligible at all. The state's own figure concedes most of the distance to that [1]. Where the university study tests behaviour it agrees: the association between job protection and taking leave is smaller at the bottom of the earnings distribution than in the middle quintiles, protection may matter less where work is already precarious, few interviewed workers named fear of job loss as a major factor, and none of the associations should be read as causal [2]. A business-side analysis reads the same series as regressive, blaming a benefit that replaces part of a wage rather than all of it [5] — a mechanism weakest where the gap is widest, since the schedule pays 90 percent at the bottom [3]. What that reading does not reach is what follows a leave: job protection is associated with a larger gain in next-quarter employment for the lowest earners than for anyone else, 5.8 points against 3.3 [2], and the study's agricultural focus group could not imagine a week off without losing their jobs [2]. Both accounts operate here.

## Coverage on paper

Coverage is the dimension on which the program did most nearly what it was written to do. The hours test counts work across any combination of employers rather than service with one, so it reaches part-time and multiple-job workers a tenure rule excludes, and 74 percent of covered workers are estimated to clear it [2][3]. The replacement schedule tilts the opposite way from most insurance, paying 90 percent of a wage at or below half the state average and 50 percent above it [3]. It is also the only law in the state offering job-protected paid leave for longer absences and new-child bonding [2], and the baseline it expanded on is unpaid: the twelve federal weeks carry no pay [5].

Coverage and realized access are separate measures, and the distance between them is where this question is actually decided. Paying the premium is not the same as clearing the hours test, and clearing the hours test is not the same as holding a right to the job at the end of the leave; the statute sets the three out in three different places [3]. The two groups with the least realized use arrive there by different routes, described below, so the participation gap is not one phenomenon with one explanation [1][4].

## What converts coverage into a leave taken

The hours test is the first gate and the widest. Workers earning under $19 an hour are a fifth of Washington's workforce but only a tenth of those with qualifying work history [1], and insufficient hours is the leading denial reason [1]. That is a coverage rule doing the work, not a decision a worker declined to make.

Job protection is the second gate and a different rule. Through 2025 it required an employer of 50 or more, twelve months of service and 1,250 hours; from January 2026 it reaches employers of 25 or more, then 15 in 2027 and eight in 2028, on a 180-day service test with no hours requirement [3]. Under the older rule 53 percent of eligible workers qualified, and holding protection is associated with taking leave: 1.8 percent of protected eligible workers claimed in a quarter against 1.1 percent of the unprotected [2]. Outreach staff describe telling workers they were eligible for the benefit but not for reinstatement [4], and neither the mandatory poster nor the optional paystub insert mentioned job protection at all [2].

## The two groups with the least realized use

The two groups are outside the program in different senses. Hourly employees at small firms are inside it — covered, premium-paying, often eligible — and until 2026 held the benefit with no statutory right to return; below eight employees they are 3 percent of those paid against 8 percent of the work-history eligible [1][2]. Self-employed workers are outside it by default and must elect in for three years and pay the entire employee premium to get inside [3]; 18 percent of those enrolled filed a claim in FY2025 [1]. The mechanisms are separate: one is a missing right attached to a benefit already held, the other a decision about whether to be covered at all [1][3].
